title: Apple Watch Fall Detection summoning help after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
summary: As a 69-year-old runner collapsed in cardiac arrest, Fall Detection on an Apple Watch Series 10 called emergency services. It alerted his emergency contacts. He made a full neurological recovery.
headline: An Apple Watch called for help after a runner’s heart stopped
metric: began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse
brief: A case report in Resuscitation Plus, published on 12 August 2026, concerns a 69-year-old man who collapsed in ventricular fibrillation while running alone. He was hidden behind a hedge on a dead-end road.[1] On detecting the fall, his Apple Watch automatically called emergency services on 112 and alerted his emergency contacts. Family members began cardiopulmonary resuscitation about 6–7 minutes after the collapse. An ambulance crew arrived about 1.5 minutes later and defibrillated him. He made a full neurological recovery. It is a single documented case, and a similar one appeared in an earlier German report. The authors document that the alerts brought his family to him. They cannot show how long he would have lain there without the alerts. That comparison rests on an interview in which a son says that he would not otherwise have found his father so quickly.[2]

headline: *Embrace* wristband alerts a mother, who calls paramedics
brief: In November 2016 a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, had an epileptic seizure. It left her unresponsive and not breathing.[1] Her Embrace wristband detected the seizure and alerted her mother, who called paramedics. The teacher survived. Her rescue rests on a single IEEE Spectrum report. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the device on 26 January 2018, after the event.[2] Later evidence comes from hospital units where patients with epilepsy are monitored. Researchers in Montreal published a study of the device in their own unit on 7 January 2026. They found that the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working. It raised 29 false alarms in 373 days of monitoring. It detected none of 510 focal seizures without convulsions, a type that the device is not cleared to detect.[3]

headline: Raebareli police arrive in 12 minutes after Meta flags a suicide post
metric: A police team reached his home within 12 minutes
brief: The Raebareli rescue preceded a similar rescue in Meerut in June 2026. Both took place under an arrangement in which Meta has alerted the Uttar Pradesh Police since 2022.[1] On 29 March 2026 an 18-year-old posted a suicide video on Instagram. Meta flagged it at about 8:58 pm and emailed the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters. The center traced his phone number and location and alerted Raebareli police. A team reached his home within 12 minutes and found an empty packet of rat poison. Police and family took him to a hospital. On 1 April 2026 police said that he was stable.[2] None of the sources says whether Meta’s classifier or a user report first flagged the post.[3] No clinician is quoted, and the type of rat poison is not reported. The claim that his life was saved therefore rests on the police account.[4] Meta’s figure for faster escalation is self-reported and dates from November 2017. At that time, the company said that reports accelerated by pattern recognition were escalated to local authorities twice as quickly as other reports.[5]

metric: 133 packets, 52.5 kg, of factory-made explosive
brief: On 20 March 2022 officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at a checkpoint in Yüksekova, Turkey. Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged the car. A hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well held 133 packets of factory-made explosive, 52.5 kg in all. The explosive was assessed as PETN-RDX.[1] The driver was a police officer posted in Istanbul. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced him to 21 years in prison for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. It sentenced four co-defendants to 17.5 years each for the same offense.[2] ASENA was designed to flag drug crime. This find lay outside its purpose. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March 2022 that police had identified a suspicious vehicle thought to be carrying drugs. He said that the police had used analysis programs, “what they call artificial intelligence”.[3] The head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department spoke in June 2022. He listed the explosives among the finds of operations that, by his account, had started with ASENA.[4] No source records the data that ASENA matched for this car. None of the sources says whether an analyst checked the flag before the stop. The driver spoke in court of “those who informed”, but no informant is reported.[5]
